The State Treasurer must publish a restricted-entity list by Oct 1, 2025 and update it at least semiannually. The bill becomes effective upon enactment. The State Treasurer must create and publish that list by October 1, 2025, and update it at least every six months. 109-1-LB663_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB663_Intro_Copy.docx LB663 amends county planning law (section 23-114.01). Key agency roles and changes:\n- Requires each county planning commission member and each county board member to complete two hours of role-specific education per term, developed and presented by the respective county attorney.\n- Requires county planning commissions and county boards to issue a statement of factual findings when granting or denying conditional-use/special-exception requests.\n- Establishes processing timelines: the commission has 30 days to assess completeness (10‑day notice for deficiencies), 30 days to reevaluate after additional information, and 90 days to decide or recommend; the board has analogous 30/10/30/90-day steps after receiving the commission’s recommendation.\n- Creates a presumption that applicants will comply with local, state, and federal requirements; challengers bear the burden of proof.\nAdministrative finance notes: members remain eligible for expense reimbursement, mileage per section 81-1176, and per diem up to $15/day not to exceed $1,000/year. No new appropriations specified. Adds a two-hour-per-term training requirement for each commission member and county board member on commissioner/board roles, with the training developed and presented by the respective county attorney. Establishes procedural rules for planning commissions and county boards: 30 days to declare an application complete (10‑day written notice if incomplete), 30 days after supplemental information to re-evaluate, and a 90‑day deadline to grant/deny or recommend action. Creates a presumption that applicants will comply with local, state, and federal requirements (burden on challengers to prove otherwise) and bars commissions/boards from conditioning a conditional use permit or special exception on obtaining other agency permits (though applicants still must secure required local, state, or federal permits). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB664_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB664_Intro_Copy.docx LB664 amends the Administrative Procedure Act (Reissue Revised Statutes §§84-906.02, 84-911). Agencies are required to permit any person to submit comments, written materials, or documentation for proposed or adopted rules or regulations, allow submissions electronically or by mail, and may not require in-person travel; agencies are also encouraged to solicit public comment via newspaper notice. The bill clarifies venue for declaratory-judgment challenges to rules: petitions may be filed in the district court of the county of the petitioner’s residence, the petitioner’s principal place of business, Lancaster County, or the county where the agency has its headquarters; the agency must be a party and may not restrict venue. Statutory procedures exclude Negotiated Rulemaking Act procedures. Original sections are repealed; the act takes effect immediately. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are provided. Adds requirements for state agencies and the district courts in administrative rule challenges: agencies must allow anyone to submit comments or supporting/opposing materials electronically or by mail and may not require in-person travel to submit them. 109-1-LB667_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB667_Final_Copy.docx LB667 amends §60-1438 of the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act to revise dealer compensation rules for diagnostic work and parts. Key agency-related provisions: dealers may establish an average parts markup by submitting sequential customer repair orders; manufacturers have 30 days to audit and 45 days after approval for the markup to take effect. A dealer may appeal a denial to the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Board, with the manufacturer bearing the burden to justify denial under the Act; an unreasonable denial is an Act violation subject to board enforcement. The bill defines compensation when a franchisor furnishes parts at no or reduced cost (uses "fair wholesale value") and preserves manufacturer/distributor audit and recall/warranty obligations. Claim/timing rules (six-month filing, 30-day approval/payment, audit periods) are clarified. Introduced in the Legislature and heard by the Transportation and Telecommunications Committee. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified. Adds rules under the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act governing dealer compensation and rate review. Key points:\n- Denials must be made pursuant to the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act.\n- When calculating part compensation, only retail sales not involving warranty repairs are used; markups for listed recommended maintenance items (oil, filters, fluids, brakes, spark plugs, wipers, tires, etc.) are excluded.\n- If a franchisor supplies a part free or at reduced cost for warranty work, the franchisor must pay the dealer the dealer's cost plus the dealer's markup, multiplied by the part's “fair wholesale value,” defined as the greatest of dealer paid amount, franchisor price-schedule cost, or cost of a substantially identical franchisor-listed part.\n- A manufacturer/distributor may request up to 100 additional dealer repair orders (from a selected 90-day window) to verify rates, may adjust payments, and dealers have 30 days to rebut; requests cannot be made more than once within 12 months.\nNo state agencies or departments (other than the cited Act) are named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. 109-1-LB686_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB686_Intro_Copy.docx LB686 prohibits Nebraska government entities and officials from knowingly keeping lists, records, or registries of privately owned firearms or firearm owners, except records maintained during criminal investigations, prosecutions, or as otherwise required by law. It also bars payment card networks and covered entities from requiring, incentivizing, or assigning merchant category codes that distinguish firearm retailers from other retailers, unless such coding is required by law. Enforcement is vested exclusively in the Nebraska Attorney General, who may investigate, issue notices to cease, seek injunctions, and request civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (with fines stayed pending appeal). No funding, appropriations, or budgetary changes are included. Adds prohibitions and an enforcement scheme enforced solely by the Attorney General. Key points:\n- Government entities may not maintain lists/registries of privately owned firearms or owners except records kept in the regular course of a criminal investigation or as otherwise required by law.\n- Payment card networks may not require or incentivize use of merchant category codes (MCCs) that distinguish firearm retailers; covered entities may not assign such distinguishing MCCs.\n- The Attorney General must investigate alleged violations (including by government entities), issue written notice, and if not remedied within 30 business days, sue for injunction. Courts must enjoin ongoing violations; continued noncompliance after 30 business days may produce civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (court to consider violator’s finances and constitutional harms). Fines are stayed on appeal. The AG has exclusive enforcement authority and the section’s remedies are exclusive. \n- No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are added. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB68_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB68_Intro_Copy.docx LB68 amends the Medical Assistance Act (adds section 3 and modifies §68-901) to require coverage and dispensing rules for self‑administered hormonal contraceptives. Private individual and group sickness and accident policies, hospital/medical/surgical expense policies, and self‑funded employee benefit plans (to the extent not preempted by federal law) must reimburse in‑network providers or dispensing entities per unit: initial prescriptions up to a three‑month supply and subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply regardless of enrollment at initial prescription. The bill prohibits requiring providers to prescribe 12‑month supplies and bars plans from imposing cost‑sharing for switching methods before exhausting a previously dispensed supply. Under the medical assistance program, the Department (administering Medicaid/family planning services) must ensure prescriptions permit one‑time dispensation of a 12‑month supply. No appropriations or budgetary allocations are included. Adds coverage requirements and a Medicaid directive. Insurers (individual/group sickness & accident, hospital/medical/surgical, and self‑funded employee plans where not federally preempted) must reimburse in‑network providers per unit for FDA‑approved self‑administered hormonal contraceptives: first prescription up to a three‑month supply; subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply even if the enrollee was not covered at the time of the first prescription. Clarifies providers are not required to prescribe 12‑month supplies and plans may not impose cost‑sharing for an alternative method if a person switches before using a dispensed supply. The state “department” administering the medical assistance (Medicaid) program must ensure a one‑time dispensation of a 12‑month supply for family planning. No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB690_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB690_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Transportation LB690 (as summarized) makes several changes affecting the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and the Department of Transportation (DOT). If plate manufacturing costs exceed the statutory charge, funds otherwise credited to the DMV Cash Fund are first applied to the Highway Trust Fund to cover the excess. Separately, sales/use tax proceeds on aircraft (transactions on/after July 1, 2023) are credited to the DOT Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund. Adds all‑terrain vehicles (ATVs) and utility‑type vehicles (UTVs) into the Motor Vehicle Registration Act when registered and operated under section 60‑6,356. Defines UTV (≤74" wide, ≤180" long, dry weight ≤2,000 lbs, four+ nonhighway tires) and excludes ATVs, golf cars, low‑speed vehicles. 109-1-LB692_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB692_Intro_Copy.docx Amends the School District Property Tax Limitation Act. The Department (responsible for calculation) must annually compute each district’s property tax request authority using a revised formula: prior-year property tax request (net of any prior-year excess) plus prior-year non-property-tax revenue minus investment income from special building funds, grown by the district’s base growth percentage, then reduced by current-year non-property-tax revenue and adjusted for documented errors. Nonproperty revenue categories lacking June 1 data default to prior-year amounts. The Department must certify the resulting authority to each school board. Changes to carryforward: districts may carry forward unused property tax request authority but must exclude increases attributable to base growth percentage under section 79-3405; the Department will calculate and report unused authority to school boards. Original sections 79-3403 and 79-3406 are repealed. No direct appropriations or new funding allocations are included. Adds language affecting school district property tax calculations: when computing the current amount, subtract any portion of last year’s property tax request that exceeded the district’s property tax request authority under section 79‑3405. Do not subtract increases to request authority that resulted from increases in the district’s base growth percentage under section 79‑3405. No specific state agencies or funding appropriations are created or changed. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB694_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB694_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Transportation The bill amends Section 39-210 (tourist-oriented directional sign panels) to require any applicant seeking qualification to provide the Department of Transportation assurance of compliance with applicable anti-discrimination laws, explicitly adding military or veteran status as a protected characteristic. 109-1-LB69_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB69_Final_Copy.docx LB69 amends statutes governing the Commission on African American Affairs. Key agency-related changes: the commission remains a 14-member body appointed by the Governor (members must be of African ancestry; initial appointments must include one immigrant/new American and one young professional); members are limited to two full four-year terms; commissioner names must be posted on the commission website; the commission elects its chair. 109-1-LB704_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB704_Final_Copy.docx LB704 amends Neb. Rev. Requires the department (child‑support agency) to initiate and complete a review when a noncustodial parent is incarcerated: parties must submit financial information (per §§43‑512.14 and 43‑512.17) within 30 days to the department and the facility administrator (per §47‑1003); the department must finish the review within 120 days and notify parties under §43‑512.13. If a decrease in support is denied, the department must schedule a conference for the incarcerated parent within 30 days (in person or virtual) and mail a notice to both parents specifying findings, format, date/time/location, evidence deadlines, waiver procedures, etc. The department must make a final determination within 30 days after the conference (or sooner if waived), decide whether to refer the order to the county or authorized attorney, and mail written notice. Notices to incarcerated parents go to the facility address and administrator. Final determinations are not contested cases under the Administrative Procedure Act. No funding or appropriation changes are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB705_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB705_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture, Department of Economic Development, Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Revenue, Department of Transportation, Military Department The bill assigns the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to establish and maintain the medical‑cannabis patient/registered‑caregiver registry, issue/renew confidential registry cards, process applications, and promulgate rules. Department of Correctional Services employees are ineligible for licenses; DCS must provide drug‑treatment to sentenced persons and receives vehicle‑lettering exemptions (shared with DHHS, Agriculture, and the Military Department). Courts must notify the Department of Motor Vehicles of certain clean‑slate orders/juvenile abstracts. Effective July 1, 2023, aircraft sale/lease sales/use tax proceeds are credited to the Department of Transportation Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund. - Department of Agriculture: Added duty to collaborate with the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission, Dept. of Revenue, and DHHS on regulation and oversight; no direct funding changes. \n- Department of Economic Development: Assigned administration of the new Medical Cannabis Business Equity Fund (may hold gifts, grants, legislative appropriations) and to run technical assistance, mentorship, and a grant program for social equity applicants and disproportionately impacted areas. 109-1-LB706_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB706_Intro_Copy.docx LB706 mandates law-enforcement dispatch screening for mental‑health indicators and requires calls identified as "Mental Health Priority" to notify and, when safe and practicable, be responded to by an APS social worker accompanying the officer; the APS social worker must lead de‑escalation and trauma‑informed interaction. The Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice (the commission) must set minimum policy standards, may provide a model policy, and will annually review agency compliance within its existing appropriations (including grants), reporting to the Governor and Legislature. Agencies with a pattern of noncompliance are ineligible for commission‑administered loans, grants, funds, or donations until corrected. Willful failure to comply can trigger discipline including revocation/suspension of officer certification. Financial enforcement: fines are collectible by the Attorney General and remitted to the State Treasurer. The bill also assigns related duties to the Department of Health and Human Services concerning APS social workers. Requires law enforcement agencies to have dispatch personnel screen calls with a checklist for mental‑health indicators, flag qualifying calls as a "Mental Health Priority," notify the nearest unit and an APS social worker, and share mental‑health information with responders. When safe/practicable, officers responding to such calls must be accompanied by an APS social worker, who will lead the interaction using de‑escalation and trauma‑informed care. Agencies must adopt written dispatch/APS‑accompaniment policies and submit them to the commission, which will set minimum standards and may distribute a model policy (not mandatory except for delinquent agencies). The commission will annually review compliance and report to the Governor and Legislature, using only existing appropriations (including any awarded grants). Agencies with patterns of noncompliance are ineligible for commission‑administered loans, grants, funds, or donations until cured. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB82_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB82_Intro_Copy.docx LB82 adopts the Cosmetology Licensure Compact, creating a multistate licensure system and a Compact Commission with an Executive Committee. The Commission may adopt binding rules, hire staff, contract services, own property, initiate litigation, and hold meetings. Financing: the Commission may accept grants/donations, levy annual assessments on Member States, and charge fees to licensees (including application and renewal fees) to fund its operations, must establish a budget, keep financial records, and obtain an annual financial review. The bill amends Neb. statutes (including sections 38-1001 and 38-1004) to incorporate the Compact. No direct state appropriations or specific Nebraska budget allocations are included. Adds creation of a Compact Commission and requires each Member State's State Licensing Authority to cooperate with it. Key governmental entities named: the Commission (and its Executive Committee), Member State State Licensing Authorities, state executive and judicial branches, governors and legislative leaders, law enforcement agencies, and federal courts (U.S. District Court for D.C. or where the Commission's principal office is located). \n\nFiscal and administrative provisions: the Commission may adopt rules, hire staff, buy/lease property, borrow, purchase insurance, and maintain a Data System. It may accept grants/donations, assess annual fees on Member States (allocated by rule) and impose fees on licensees to fund operations, establish a budget, keep audited financial records, and cannot pledge Member State credit without approval. 109-1-LB94_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB94_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Economic Development, Department of Labor The bill directs the Department of Labor, in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development, to: establish two grant programs—(1) up to $20 million per fiscal year for local educational institutions/nonprofits to develop digital skills training centers in qualified census tracts; and (2) up to $20 million per fiscal year to cover tuition, materials, transportation, equipment, and child care for low-income individuals attending such centers. The Department of Labor, with Economic Development and industry input, must develop standardized, industry‑aligned curricula (core skills, specialty tracks, and bootcamps) and shall partner with technology employers to support apprenticeships, job placement, advancement, and outreach. The Legislature intends to appropriate $50 million annually from the Workforce Development Program Cash Fund to the Department of Labor beginning FY2025‑26 for grants under the Digital Skills Empowerment Act. Section 81‑407 is amended to authorize the Department of Labor to administer the Fund for these grants. 109-1-LB99_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB99_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services This bill amends definitions and directs duties for the Department of Correctional Services. It codifies “Department” and “Director of Correctional Services,” treats committed offenders and facilities as those under the department, and defines “restrictive housing.” It requires the department to limit use of restrictive housing (no more than 15 consecutive days; single-occupancy cells unless inmates consent), to adopt Administrative Procedure Act rules establishing restrictive-housing levels, placement criteria, and individualized transition plans developed with the committed offender. The department must promulgate rules addressing risks for vulnerable populations (bar placement in restrictive housing except for immediate segregation pending classification) and may develop secure mental-health housing that ensures meaningful access to social interaction, exercise, stimulation, and therapeutic programming. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Added provisions restrict use of restrictive housing: inmates may not be held in restrictive housing for more than 15 consecutive days, and single‑occupancy cells cannot hold more than one inmate unless all inmates voluntarily agree in writing. The bill adds definitions relevant to placement decisions and care: developmental disability, “member” (fragmented), serious mental illness (broad medical definition with examples: schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, delusional disorder, bipolar disorder, major depression, OCD), and traumatic brain injury (fragmented). No appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations for the Department of Correctional Services are included in the added text. Operational policy, screening, and housing practices for the Department would likely require revision. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB9_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB9_Final_Copy.docx LB9 adds regulation and taxation of alternative nicotine products, electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS), and defined "nicotine analogues." Key state actors and fiscal provisions:\n\n- Tax Commissioner: expanded enforcement and reporting powers under the cigarette tax division and Tobacco Products Tax Act — requires monthly manufacturer/importer/stamping-agent reports, examines returns, issues deficiency notices (3-year rule; 6 years for fraud), may suspend/revoke licenses, impose administrative penalties (up to $1,000 for cigarette-related violations; up to $5,000 under the Tobacco Products Tax Act), and direct seizure/forfeiture of contraband tobacco/ENDS without warrant. \n- Attorney General: may seek injunctions on behalf of the Tax Commissioner and recover investigation/action costs and attorney fees. \n- Governor: advises/consents to Tax Commissioner hiring; county attorneys, sheriffs, and peace officers may assist enforcement. \n- Fiscal impacts: snuff taxed 44¢/oz; ENDS ≤3 ml at $0.05/ml, >3 ml at 10% of price; alternative nicotine and most other tobacco products taxed at 20% of price. Adds definitions for "nicotine analogue" and ties "alternative nicotine product" to section 28-1418.01. Assigns a 20% tax on alternative nicotine products based on the first owner's purchase price or resale price. Expands enforcement authority of the Nebraska Tax Commissioner: examine returns promptly, issue deficiency notices (generally within 3 years, 6 years for fraud/large omissions), and accept written extensions of the assessment period. Authorizes administrative sanctions—license suspension/revocation (under sections 28-1420 to 28-1429 and the Administrative Procedure Act) and penalties up to $5,000. 109-2-LB1032_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1032_Final_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill assigns extensive duties to the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). DHHS may recommend termination/referral for adoption (or tribal customary adoption for eligible Indian children), perform medical assessments of adoptive placements, and maintain current placement contact information. DHHS may make post‑adoption maintenance/medical payments (ending by age 20), pay specified treatment costs, and reimburse up to $2,000 for nonrecurring special‑needs adoption expenses. For Indian children, DHHS must notify parents/tribes within five days, provide remedial services until unsuccessful, submit specified court information when involved, notify tribes within 30 days if concurrent tribal jurisdiction is granted, and may adopt implementing rules. Courts may ask the DHHS secretary to pay attorney fees "out of funds which may be appropriated." The additions expand Department of Health and Human Services (the department) duties regarding tribal customary adoptions. Key changes: DHHS may recommend referral for tribal customary adoption (and, if it does, must not recommend termination of parental rights); within 30 days after a state court grants temporary concurrent jurisdiction to a tribe, DHHS must notify the tribe about required elements/documents for state acceptance, provide the tribe and proposed adoptive parents a written report on the child (medical, educational, developmental, tribal affiliation information where permitted), and provide copies of court filings. The department will consult on finalizing adoption assistance agreements and may adopt rules and regulations to implement these provisions. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB1036_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1036_Intro_Copy.docx LB1036 (2026) amends Nebraska Evid. R. §27-404 to permit admission of evidence of other crimes, wrongs, or acts when such evidence is "inextricably intertwined" with the charged offense or for other recognized non‑propensity purposes (motive, intent, identity, etc.). The bill defines "inextricably intertwined" by three criteria (part of the factual setting; so blended that proof of the charged offense requires proof of the other acts; or necessary to present a coherent picture). In criminal cases, the prosecution must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the accused committed the other act and, when relevant, that it is inextricably intertwined; proof must be shown outside the jury's presence, and the court shall give a limiting instruction on request. If offered under the specified subdivision, the prosecution must show the intertwinement, and upon the defendant’s request the court must give a limiting jury instruction. 109-2-LB1130_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1130_Intro_Copy.docx Creates a Community Improvement District (CID) framework assigning clear duties to state and local officials. City and village councils and clerks process CID formation, plans, levies, and filings; CID clerks must file annexation/dissolution/merger/resolution documents with city/village clerks and the Secretary of State and notify county clerks, election commissioners, and registers of deeds. County clerks receive levies/filings; registers of deeds record boundaries. County treasurers serve ex officio as CID treasurers, establish CID funds/accounts, collect CID taxes and special assessments, segregate funds, and disburse per court‑approved compromise settlements. Election commissioners or county clerks administer trustee elections (sealed mail ballots) and act as recall filing clerks; the Secretary of State supplies uniform recall papers. CIDs must file annual budgets and audits with the Auditor of Public Accounts by Dec. 31; the Auditor may waive audits, appoint an administrator (who assumes board powers), or assess liens if noncompliant. Key agencies and duties:\n- City/village councils/boards: approve CID formation, plans, levy caps, annexations, amendments, and accept improvements.\n- County treasurer: serves ex officio as CID treasurer, establishes CID funds/accounts, collects/deposits taxes and special assessments, and disburses funds per trustees/administrator.\n- County clerk, register of deeds, and election commissioner: receive filings/notice of CID actions, elections, annexations, dissolutions, mergers, and detachment.\n- Auditor of Public Accounts: receives annual budgets and audits, may waive audits, access records, can be referred by district court to appoint an administrator for troubled CIDs.\n- District court: reviews contest/compromise of warrants/bonds and may order levy adjustments; approves bond/warrant compromises.\n- Secretary of State: designs uniform recall petition papers; filing clerk (election commissioner/county clerk) manages recall/election procedures.\n\nFunding changes: CIDs may levy a property tax up to a stated per-$100 cap (placeholder) to fund general corporate purposes and debt service; audit and bond premium costs are paid from CID funds; Auditor can require/arrange audits with fees becoming liens. No state agencies are assigned new duties, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. Establishes court procedures to adjudicate parentage, limits a child to two parents, lists best-interest and equity factors (and special genetic‑testing considerations), time limits and conditions for a spouse to challenge parentage, and exclusions for births by sexual intercourse, surrogacy agreements, and the Nebraska Indian Child Welfare Act. Stat. §13-3206 (Property Assessed Clean Energy Act) to revise PACE lien procedures and priorities. Municipalities must record a PACE lien in the county register of deeds within 14 days after an annual assessment becomes delinquent (or within 14 days of notice from a third-party lender), certify the delinquency to the county treasurer, and the lien is treated as a special assessment collected under Chapter 77 (sections 77-1801 to 77-1863, including 77-1858). For single-family residential property the initial assessment creates a lien recorded upon imposition; residential PACE liens are subordinate to prior-recorded liens and to a first mortgage recorded after the PACE notice and have priority over other subsequently recorded liens. Nonresidential PACE liens require a recorded consent/subordination per §13-3205 to attain parity with tax liens. Foreclosure proceeds follow these priorities; delinquent assessments may be satisfied from the loss reserve fund (§13-3208) or extinguished if proceeds are insufficient. Loan servicers may raise escrow payments to cover PACE assessments. The bill repeals the original section and takes effect immediately (emergency). If a third‑party lender notifies a municipality that an annual assessment for an energy project is delinquent, the municipality must, within 14 days, certify the delinquent amount and lien to the county treasurer. The lien will be treated as a special assessment under section 77-1858 and collected using the same county treasurer procedures and real estate tax/special assessment processes set out in Chapter 77 (sections 77-1801 to 77-1863). Clerks and counties must provide monthly data and may enter written agreements with the department to receive reimbursement for costs. The department must promulgate rules on reimbursement rates and methods, accounting for federal funds and any legislative appropriations; reimbursement funds are to be added to county budgets and carried over. DHHS-administered processes allow support obligations to start as early as the month of conception (physician-determined) if the mother requests, permit retroactive collection (including when paternity is later established), and require court-set payment amounts based on the mother’s and child’s best interests. DHHS-related actions to establish paternity require the mother’s consent and must not be undertaken if they pose risk of harm to the unborn child. 109-2-LB757_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB757_Intro_Copy.docx LB757 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §77-2704.28 to create a sales and use tax exemption (under the Nebraska Revenue Act of 1967) for the purchase of an aircraft that will be leased between related entities (parent/subsidiary, subsidiary/subsidiary, or brother‑sister companies). The exemption applies only if (1) annual gross receipts from leasing the aircraft (including related-party leases) equal at least 7.5% of the aircraft’s net acquisition price (including trade value, excluding third‑party sales commissions) and (2) sales tax is collected and remitted on the lease payments. The act becomes operative October 1, 2026, and repeals the original section. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds a sales-and-use-tax exemption under the Nebraska Revenue Act of 1967 for purchases of aircraft intended for lease, including transfers between parent/subsidiary, sister, or related companies, provided two conditions are met: (1) annual gross receipts from leasing the aircraft (including related‑party leases) are at least 7.5% of the aircraft’s net acquisition price (counting trade/exchange value but excluding third‑party sales commissions), and (2) sales tax is collected and remitted on the lease payments. No specific state agency or department is named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB758_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB758_Final_Copy.docx LB758 amends Nebraska statutes to create a statutory mechanism enabling 501(c)(3) charitable organizations to present a notarized affidavit (with an IRS determination letter or group exemption proof, state certificate of existence, death evidence, corporate resolution, and Form W‑9) to holders of decedents’ property or to persons with information to obtain property or information. Holders must pay, deliver, or transfer property (except trust/estate distributions) or provide requested information; complying persons are discharged as if dealing with a personal representative. Charities gain a right of action if property is not transferred within 45 days or information not provided within 30 days unless a timely notice of reasonable delay (e.g., court order or federal banking/AML law conflicts) is given. The affidavit is added as acceptable evidence of ownership for vehicle certificate-of-title applications (affecting the Department and county treasurers). No funding or appropriation changes. Original sections are repealed. Adds a process allowing 501(c)(3) charitable organizations to present a sworn affidavit to a holder of a decedent's property (or a person with information about it) to obtain payment, transfer, delivery, or information about the asset. Key government references: the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — the affidavit must include the charity's IRS determination or group-exemption evidence and a completed IRS Form W‑9 — and citations to federal statutes/regulations (12 U.S.C. provisions, 31 U.S.C. provisions, and 31 C.F.R. 1000–1019) as legitimate bases for a financial institution to delay or refuse compliance. Sets deadlines (45 days for transfer; 30 days for information) and permits judicial action for noncompliance. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB765_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB765_Intro_Copy.docx LB765 amends school-bond and joint-entity bond law. Key state/local entities affected: boards of education, Nebraska school districts, educational service units (ESUs), county clerks, election commissioners, and county canvassing boards (Election Act procedures apply). For school-district bonds the bill requires submission to qualified electors, a turnout threshold of at least 50.1% of qualified electors, and a majority favoring issuance; filing deadlines for bond orders at statewide primary/general elections are specified. For joint entities (created on/after Feb 14, 2024) that include a Nebraska school district or ESU, similar per-district elector submission, 50.1% turnout, and majority-approval requirements apply; notice must be given at least 50 days prior. The bill prohibits use of public funds (including building, cash, and discretionary funds) to support bond campaigns, bars paid employee advocacy time, and bans campaign materials on school/ESU property. Original sections are repealed. Adds prohibitions affecting school districts and educational service units (and joint entities that include them). Public funds — including building funds, cash funds, and discretionary funds — may not be used to establish, support, promote, underwrite, subsidize, or otherwise advocate for campaigns to influence voters in school- or joint-entity bond elections; privately raised funds (e.g., concessions, booster clubs, PTOs) are excluded. District/ESU employees may not use paid work time on such campaigning but may provide neutral informational details (subject, amount, date). Campaign materials advocating for bonds may not be posted or distributed on school/ESU property. No new appropriations or budget increases are made; this imposes spending restrictions. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB823_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB823_Final_Copy.docx LB823 amends Nebraska’s land‑management burning statutes. It clarifies that local fire chiefs may waive the statewide open‑burning ban by issuing permits and specifies required permit information (including the responsible person's contact, designation as prescribed or controlled burn, and approximate acreage). The State Fire Marshal must post a sample permit form online. Fire chiefs may delegate most permit duties to department members but not the authority to adopt local permit‑issuance standards. Applicants must file detailed burn plans; permits are valid up to 30 days. Local fire departments may charge up to $10 per permit; fees are remitted to the governing body for inclusion in the fire department’s general funds and shall not reduce the department’s tax requirements. Adds a provision (effective Jan. 1, 2026) tying the state subtraction from federal adjusted gross income to federal rules: individuals who itemized on their federal return may subtract the greater of the state standard deduction or their federal itemized deductions (per IRC §63(d)), but the portion for state/local income taxes is limited by the applicable cap in IRC §164(b)(7) for taxable years beginning after 2029, using that section as it existed on Jan. 1, 2026. The text cites the Internal Revenue Code (federal tax law, administered by the IRS/Treasury). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB847_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB847_Final_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services, Department of Economic Development, Department of Labor, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Revenue The bill makes multiple changes affecting the Department of Labor (DOL), Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), and Department of Revenue (DOR). 109-2-LB977_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB977_Final_Copy.docx LB977 revises Nebraska’s Rules of the Road and clarifies the roles of state and local authorities. 109-2-LB978_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB978_Intro_Copy.docx This bill creates a new statutory civil cause of action targeting persons who create, distribute, or otherwise enable access to defined "prohibited content" (obscene materials, child sexual abuse materials, child sexual exploitation devices/images). Enforcement and remedies: the Attorney General and county attorneys may seek injunctions, equitable relief, and civil penalties (up to $10,000 per violation). Sovereign immunity is not an affirmative defense. Collected civil penalties are remitted to the State Treasurer for distribution in accordance with Article VII, §5 of the Nebraska Constitution. The bill grants specified immunities: Internet utilities (for passive provision of access), courts, attorneys, and their agents/employees, and limited protections for judges viewing/possessing prohibited content in good-faith official contexts. The statute supplements—rather than replaces—other remedies and applies regardless of publisher status or criminal conviction. No explicit appropriations or new budget allocations are provided. Adds enforcement and penalty provisions: the Nebraska Attorney General and county attorneys may bring civil actions to restrain or enjoin violations and recover civil penalties (up to $10,000 per violation). Sovereign immunity is not an affirmative defense, and remedies may be awarded regardless of a criminal conviction. Internet utilities are shielded from liability for merely providing access, transmission, storage, or connection to content they did not help create or develop. Judges acting in good faith in the course of official duties are exempt from liability for viewing/possession of prohibited content. Collected civil penalties must be remitted to the State Treasurer for distribution under Neb. Const. Art. VII, §5. No separate appropriations or new agency budget allocations are specified. 109-2-LB995_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB995_Intro_Copy.docx LB995 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§43-272, 43-279, and 43-3102 to strengthen appointment-of-counsel and waiver protections in juvenile court. Juvenile courts must appoint counsel when petitions allege jurisdiction under specified subdivisions and must provide parties written, youth‑friendly materials explaining the right to counsel. The Nebraska Supreme Court is directed to adopt standards/guidelines and a rule‑based process to ensure juveniles can consult with counsel before waiving counsel. Waivers must be made in open court, recorded, signed, affirmative, and evaluated for age, intelligence, emotional stability, and case complexity; juveniles must receive the written materials. Parents/others may not waive the juvenile’s right; waiver is categorically barred in certain proceedings (e.g., under‑14 juveniles, detention hearings, dispositional hearings seeking out‑of‑home placement, transfer motions). Counties bear appointed counsel costs when families cannot afford counsel; courts may later order parental reimbursement under existing collection procedures. No new appropriations are included. Added provisions require juvenile courts to advise juveniles and their parent/guardian of the right to counsel at subsequent hearings and to inquire whether they wish to retain counsel. Courts must provide each juvenile and parent/guardian with written materials explaining the juvenile’s right to counsel; the materials must be written at a level understandable to the juvenile and developed using best practices to ensure comprehension. The bill also adds documentary/waiver conditions (including that the juvenile has been provided the required written materials). No executive agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations in the added text. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB996_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB996_Intro_Copy.docx LB996 restricts the use of mechanical restraints on juveniles and amends provisions governing juvenile transportation policies. Key agency impacts:\n\n- Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS): DHHS policies and procedures on transporting juveniles placed at youth rehabilitation and treatment centers must prohibit shackling as defined in the bill and ban the routine use of mechanical restraints during transport. Exceptions must be narrowly tailored, documented in writing, and subject to review.\n- Office of Juvenile Services (OJS): DHHS transportation policies apply to any private contractor used by OJS to transport juveniles at youth rehabilitation and treatment centers.\n- The bill adds a statutory definition of "shackling" and limits permissible use to situations with recent behavior showing substantial risk, no less-restrictive alternative, and only for the strictly necessary duration.\n\nNo changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds a prohibition on shackling juveniles except when an authorized person reasonably determines a juvenile poses a substantial, recent risk of physical harm, no less‑restrictive alternative exists, and shackling is limited to the strictly necessary duration. Defines “shackling” (handcuffs, leg irons, waist/belly chains, restraint chair, etc.) but allows brief, temporary handcuffs for immediate articulable risk. Excludes restraints governed by section 43-251.03. Requires policies to bar shackling that violates this section and to prohibit routine mechanical restraints during juvenile transportation; any exceptions must be narrowly limited, documented in writing, and subject to review. No specific government agencies or departments are named and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are added. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB997_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB997_Intro_Copy.docx LB997 amends §73-815 of the State Procurement Act governing sole-source service contracts over $50,000. It preserves preapproval by the procurement division except in emergencies, where approval by the state agency director (or designee) suffices. Within three business days after emergency contract approval, the state agency must provide the contract and its written justification to the Director of Administrative Services and to the Auditor of Public Accounts, and retain a copy in its files. The Director of Administrative Services is directed to maintain a complete record of such sole-source contracts. The bill repeals the original §73-815. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are made. Adds the Auditor of Public Accounts as a recipient (i.e., requires copies be provided to that office). No other agencies are named and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are addressed. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB998_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB998_Final_Copy.docx LB998 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §77-2716 to expand Nebraska income tax exclusions for members of the Nebraska National Guard. For taxable years beginning 2025–2026, Guard members may exclude 100% of income from specified 32 U.S.C. duty statuses (e.g., drills, annual training, AGR or ADOS), employment as 32 U.S.C. federal dual‑status technicians with the Nebraska National Guard, and state active duty. Beginning January 1, 2027, the exclusion is extended to income earned while serving in either 10 U.S.C. or 32 U.S.C. military duty status, dual‑status technician employment, or state active duty. The Department of Revenue (Tax Commissioner) continues to administer the income tax modifications. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are contained in the bill. Adds a state income-tax exclusion, effective for taxable years beginning or deemed to begin on or after January 1, 2027: members of the Nebraska National Guard may exclude 100% of income (to the extent included in federal adjusted gross income) from three sources — service in 10 U.S.C. or 32 U.S.C. military duty status while a Nebraska National Guard member; employment as a 32 U.S.C. federal dual‑status technician with the Nebraska National Guard; and service in state active duty. References Internal Revenue Code and U.S. Code sections; no funding or appropriation changes. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB999_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB999_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Economic Development, Department of Labor The bill does not explicitly reference the Department of Economic Development or the Department of Labor. It creates a Business Innovation and Startup Fund, consisting of funds transferred by the Legislature, to be used by the newly established Business Innovation and Startup Commission; monies available for investment are to be managed by the state investment officer under existing state investment laws. The commission must report annually to the Legislature (beginning December 1, 2027) including an accounting of grant awards and other financial assistance. No appropriations or budget allocations to the two named departments are specified. No direct changes are made to the Department of Economic Development or the Department of Labor in the added text. The amendment creates a Business Innovation and Startup Fund (financed by legislative transfers; no amounts specified) and a Business Innovation and Startup Commission to implement the Act. Fund assets may be invested by the state investment officer under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. The Commission must begin annual electronic reporting to the Legislature by Dec. 1, 2027, covering activities, grant accounting, ecosystem progress, measurable outcomes (startup formation, access to capital, geographic and underserved-community participation), and statutory/regulatory/budget recommendations. No explicit appropriations or budget allocations to DED or Dept. of Labor are specified. DOCX | PDF
LB319_Intro_Copy.docx Unknown session Legislative Bill 319 delegates several responsibilities to the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). The Department is tasked with maximizing federal funding to minimize the use of state General Funds for SNAP and is required to employ necessary personnel to explore available federal options for Nebraska.\n\nAdditional provisions include the development of a state outreach plan conforming to the Food and Nutrition Service's criteria, which is part of the United States Department of Agriculture. DHHS may seek gifts, grants, or donations to fund the outreach initiative, which must be submitted to the Food and Nutrition Service for approval. If approved, it may secure federal matching funds, aiming to supplement state funds for increased caseloads due to the outreach plan implementation.\n\nThe bill explicitly prohibits the use of General Funds by the Department of Labor for any action regarding a SNAP benefit partnership program, focused on encouraging higher employment among recipients. This program requires no state General Funds but may act with federal or other non-state funding. \n\nLastly, the DHHS is mandated to provide annual reports detailing the efficiencies and costs of these implementations to the Health and Human Services Committee of the Legislature. The legislative text modifies eligibility criteria for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) related to individuals convicted of felonies involving controlled substances. According to the new provisions under 21 U.S.C. 862, individuals convicted of such felonies will now be eligible for SNAP benefits only if they have either completed their sentence or are currently serving parole, probation, or post-release supervision. This change pertains to policies administered by the Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP. The amendment does not include any direct changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations within the specified departments. —
